Apollo Global Management (NYSE:APO) has traded only about $22 billion in private credit assets since launching its private credit trading desk earlier this month.

John Cortese, partner and co-head of corporate credit at Apollo, told Bloomberg that the private credit desk has traded approximately 300 assets with 90 counterparties. Only about 10% of that volume involved loans originated by other firms, with the remainder coming from Apollo's own originations.

Apollo Pushes Into Private-Credit Trading

Apollo began rolling out weekly marks, not daily ones, across its approximately $600 billion credit business this month. The company says the trading desk is a pilot meant to test demand for private credit liquidity, rather than a full push to open the market.

"It's unlikely investors will need this kind of liquidity anytime soon. Most of them are comfortable with quarterly valuations and the privacy they bring," said Cortese.

The SEC recently released a statement saying that managers can rely on quarterly valuations when borrower information is limited, provided they document their reasoning.

The SEC staff indicated that limited borrower information is an acceptable basis for keeping valuations unchanged, as long as the rationale is disclosed.

Cortese told Bloomberg that the desk is unlikely to expand beyond its current scope, and that the firm sees little benefit in greater transparency for private credit investors.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) has reportedly abandoned plans for a $40 billion financing package and will instead fund its Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) chip purchases with about $8 billion of equity, led by Goldman Sachs.

Cortese said that large companies are generally avoiding private-credit solutions for AI infrastructure and chip development, and that he expects that activity to decline.

Apollo is not expected to lead any part of the transaction. The deal, if it proceeds, is expected to close in 2026 rather than 2027.
headline: Apollo's Private Credit Trading Desk Trades Just $22 Billion; Most Volume Is Its Own Loans
summary: Apollo says its private credit desk has traded about $22 billion, mostly on its own loans, and that the SpaceX chip financing has been replaced by an equity raise.
